1:
Deborah is named first, Gill says, because as Kimchi puts it she was the root or foundation of the work, chief both in the direction of the war and in the composition of the song; Ben Gersom observes that she alone composed it, and the verb is singular — then sang Deborah — after which, and in her words, Barak sang also, joining not in making the song but in singing it, as the people likewise joined, as they had with Moses at the Red Sea. Ellicott makes the same division and adds why it was fitting: she was a prophetess, and the word for prophet, like the Latin vates, involved gifts closely allied to the poet's, so that though Deborah was doubtless sole author, as the singular verb implies, Barak joined in antiphon when it was sung, as Moses at the head of the warriors and Miriam at the head of the women sang the song of Exodus. Henry finds her authorship confirmed by the later line, till I Deborah arose, and would render the opening words, Then she sang, even Deborah. She used her power as a princess as well as her gifts as a prophetess, obliging the conquering army to learn and sing it — not that they should celebrate her praises, but join with her in magnifying God: she had been the first wheel in the action, and is now the first in the thanksgiving.

Clarke warns the reader before he begins: there are many difficulties in this very sublime song, and several gross mistakes in our version will be instantly acknowledged by all who can critically examine the original. Kennicott distributed it into parts assigned to Deborah and Barak alternately, but that division is by far too artificial; Hales's version perhaps comes nearer the simplicity of the original, though it too leaves several difficulties behind. Keil has no such hesitation about the poem itself: it is so direct and lively an utterance of the enthusiasm awakened by the exaltation of Israel and its victory over Sisera that its genuineness is now generally admitted. He also lays out its plan: after a general summons to praise the Lord for the courage with which the people rose to fight, a first section dilates on the significance of the victory — the glorious times when Israel was exalted to be the nation of the Lord, the disgraceful decline of more recent times, and the joyful turn that followed Deborah's appearance — and then, after a fresh summons, a second gives a lively picture of the conflict.

The second verse turns on a disputed word, over which the two grammarians divide. Keil reports that many, following the Septuagint, give it the sense of beginning or leading, and try to establish that from an Arabic word signifying to find oneself at the head of an affair; but it cannot be established in Hebrew, since the verb means only to let loose, and in the one other place where the noun occurs it refers not to a leader but to the luxuriant growth of the hair as a sign of great strength. He therefore renders it comati, the hairy ones, those who possessed strength — the champions who went before the nation in the fight. Ellicott takes the other side, holding that the Hebrew cannot bear the sense of avenging at all, though the Syriac has it and the Chaldee implies it, and that the Septuagint are right with in the leading of the leaders of Israel; for whether the notion is that of nobles who wear long hair, like Homer's long-haired Greeks, or of hairy champions, or of warriors' hair streaming as they rode, leadership seems to be involved, and God is praised because leaders and people alike did their duty. Gill keeps the received rendering, referring the vengeance to the injuries done Israel by Jabin these twenty years past.
3:
The kings and princes summoned to listen are not Israel's, which had no kings at that time, but those of the heathen nations, as in the second psalm; Keil says they were to discern the mighty acts of Jehovah and learn to fear Him as almighty God, and notes that the verb Deborah uses is the technical term for singing with instrumental accompaniment. Ellicott makes the same identification and notes that the Septuagint render princes by satraps, the Chaldee referring the summons to the kings allied with Jabin. Gill widens it as far as it will go: not the neighbouring potentates only but all the kings of the earth, in succeeding ages too, that they might learn there is one higher than they and be cautious how they oppress the people of God — the Targum restricting it to the kings who came with Sisera, Kimchi noting that some refer it to Israel, who were all the sons of kings.

Where the march out of Seir points is the chapter's first division. Clarke takes it for the giving of the law and the manifestation of God's power and glory at that time, the most signal display of his majesty and mercy toward their forefathers, with which Deborah very properly begins. Gill reports both readings: the Targum and Jarchi refer it to Sinai, Aben Ezra and Kimchi to the Lord's going before Israel after they had encompassed Edom and marched toward Canaan, when they fought Sihon and Og and struck terror into the nations round about. Ellicott argues the second case hard. The majority of commentators, ancient and modern, suppose the promulgation of the law is meant, but the mention of Seir and Edom seems to show it is not, the imagery is different, and the context requires a more pertinent allusion; the train of thought is clearer if the march from Kadesh Barnea to their first great conquest east of Jordan is intended, signalised by the same majestic natural phenomena which had helped them defeat Sisera — and though the earthquakes and rains that made so deep an impression are not recorded in the Pentateuch, the memory of them survives in this passage and two others. Keil keeps the older view, hearing an unmistakable allusion to Moses' blessing and making the manifestation at Sinai the starting-point of Deborah's praise.

Against that glorification Keil sets the dark reverse, the degradation into which Israel sank by falling away into idolatry; Henry itemises the ruin. There was no trade, for want of soldiers to protect men of business and magistrates to restrain robbers, so that commerce ceased; no travelling, since robbers insulted on the open roads while honest travellers skulked through byways in continual frights; no tillage, the farmers quitting houses that were continually plundered for the shelter of walled cities; no justice, there being war in the gates where the courts were kept; and neither arms nor spirit, not a shield or spear seen among forty thousand, since they were either disarmed by their oppressors or had let their weapons rust for want of skill and will to use them. The cause he puts in one word — they chose new gods. The Lord their God was one Lord, but that would not content them; their God was the Ancient of days, still the same, and so they grew weary of him and must have gods of their own choosing, being as fond of them as children of new clothes. Ellicott renders the desolate roads literally as keeping holiday, the grass growing on them for want of anyone to occupy them, and the travellers as walkers of paths who slink along by tortuous, devious lanes; and he quotes a traveller in America reminded of the verse by the neutral ground in 1780: houses plundered, enclosures broken down, cattle carried away, fields waste, the roads grass-grown, the country mournful, solitary, silent.
7:
The word behind the inhabitants of the villages is uncertain, and Ellicott lays out the case. Our version's rendering is supported by the Chaldee and by analogous words elsewhere, but it cannot be the sense in the eleventh verse, and it is more probable that the Septuagint is right in rendering it princes, the Vulgate having the strong ones — though the difficulty of the term is shown by the Alexandrine manuscript simply transliterating it. Warlike chiefs is probably the sense; Luther makes them peasants. Gill takes the received sense and fills in the picture: the Canaanite robbers did not only go upon the highway but entered the villages and unwalled towns and plundered the houses, so that the inhabitants quit their dwellings for the fortified cities, and the villages were left empty and in time fell to ruin. Clarke says the same in a sentence: the people had to live together in fortified places, or in great numbers, to protect each other against bands of spoilers. Keil supplies what war at the gates means: the enemy pressed up to the very gates of the Israelite towns and besieged them, and the question about shield and spear is put in the form that assumes a negative answer, no warriors having ventured to defend the land.

The Vulgate reads the opening clause quite differently — the Lord chose a new species of war, and himself subverted the gates of the enemy — and Clarke, instead of dismissing it, asks what such a war would look like, and finds the answer in the narrative. A woman signifies her orders to Barak; he takes ten thousand men, wholly unarmed, and retires to Mount Tabor, where they are besieged by a powerful and well-appointed army; on a sudden Barak and his men rush upon them, terror spreads through the whole Canaanite host, and the rout is instantaneous; the Israelites arm themselves with their enemies' arms, Sisera is no longer safe in his chariot but flies away on foot, and the whole army is destroyed. Ellicott weighs the same variant as a textual question and decides against it. The Chaldee and the Septuagint support the reading of our version, which the song of Moses strongly confirms, whereas the Syriac and Vulgate give a poorer sense and are open to the objection that Jehovah, not Elohim, is used throughout the rest of the song.

Whether Israel had been disarmed he also disputes. The clause is usually and not unnaturally explained of a general disarmament, in which case we must assume they had only bows, slings and swords; but there is no indication, and rather the reverse, that Barak's army was unarmed — and it numbered ten thousand, not forty thousand — so the context rather favours the meaning that not a warrior in all Israel dared put on his armour. The number itself he finds remarkable even as a round one, for the Transjordanic tribes alone had sent forty thousand men to help Joshua in the conquest of Canaan, so that the figure shows how weakened and disunited Israel had become. On the governors whom Deborah's heart goes out to, Gill reports that most of the Jewish commentators, and the Targum, understand the wise men and scribes who were willing to teach the people the law even in times of trouble, while Kimchi and Ben Melech understand the great men of the nation, the nobles and rulers who enacted good laws or saw the good laws they had executed. Ellicott renders the word law-givers, finds Deborah's gratitude in the bare fact that even in this extremity Israel had men willing to brave any danger to rescue their people, and adds that when the leaders moved the people moved with them; Keil takes her heart to be drawn toward them, and has leaders and willing ones alike praise the Lord for crowning their willingness.
10:
The imperative that opens the verse Ellicott would render Think of it, or Meditate the song, noting that in the original it stands at the end of the line, far more forcibly placed. On the white asses he is emphatic that the colour word is wrong, since there are no white asses; it means rather bright-coloured, glossy-skinned or dappled, and these were the more valuable sort, used by the rich and great. Because that was not understood among the Greeks and Romans, who despised the ass, the Septuagint and Josephus often disguise the word for Gentile readers, putting steed or beast of burden in its place — no incident being more derided among the Gentiles than the riding to Zion of her king, meek and sitting upon an ass. Gill makes the same point from the Judean side. In some countries riding an ass is disgraceful, and Leo Africanus mentions an African preacher called the ass rider because he was continually sitting on one; but in Judea, where horses were few, it was accounted honourable, as in our Lord's day, and we read of the numerous sons of two judges who rode on asses' colts. He adds that the Hebrew name of the animal comes from redness, the usual colour in those parts, for which reason asses were hateful to the Egyptians, their Typhon being of that colour.

Keil reads the verse as a summons to the whole nation by classes. Those who ride upon white — that is, white-spotted — asses are the upper classes, not merely the leaders; those who sit upon coverings are the rich and prosperous; and those who walk on the way, travellers on foot, are the middle and lower classes, who go about and attend to their affairs. He grants the division is not exact, the first two terms forming no true antithesis. Ellicott takes the middle term the same way, preferring ye that sit on rich divans to ye that sit in judgment, though he records that some Jews read the Hebrew as at Middin, the town in Judah, which they supposed peculiarly oppressed by the enemy, that others make it saddle-cloths, and that the Alexandrine manuscript has sedans or covered chariots; bright carpets, he concludes, is almost certainly the sense. Clarke would render the asses sleek or well-fed, as the Vulgate has shining asses, and takes those who walk by the way for persons going from place to place for traffic.

Why the wells should be places of terror Clarke explains from the geography. Wells being scarce in every part of the East, and travellers in such hot countries needing water, robbers took their stations near tanks, pools and springs, to fall suddenly on those who came to drink, and where a country was badly governed such annoyances were frequent; Dr. Shaw describes a beautiful rill running into a basin of Roman workmanship called drink and be off, from the danger of meeting assassins there. Instead of that insecurity, Deborah intimates that they may now sit down at the watering place and there rehearse the righteous acts of the Lord. Gill offers the alternatives — the army delivered from Sisera's archers at the Kishon, the maidens frightened at the wells, the shepherds repulsed as they watered their flocks — and a rendering that makes it the voice of those who number sheep and cattle at the watering places, which they could now do again in peace. Ellicott admits the meaning is highly uncertain: they that are delivered is a conjectural addition of our version, the Hebrew having only from the noise; the Vulgate renders it where the chariots clashed together and the army of the enemy was strangled; the Chaldee is utterly vague; and Ewald has from the shoutings of the spoil-dividers between the water-troughs. Amid these uncertainties, he says, we have nothing better to offer than the conjecture of our translators.
12:
The fourfold call to awake is read by the commentators as a self-summons of two kinds. Henry hears in it both the sense Deborah had of the excellency and difficulty of the work, which well deserved the utmost liveliness and vigour of soul, all the faculties employed in their closest intensity, and the sense of her own infirmity and aptness to flag in her zeal — praising God being work that we should awake to, and awake ourselves to. Gill puts the same alternatives more plainly: either she perceived some languor in her spirits while delivering the song, and rouses herself to attend the service with more ardour, or rather, finding herself the more impressed with the great and good things the Lord had done for Israel, she calls upon her soul to exert all its powers, and for that reason repeats the word so often. Keil and Ellicott agree that the verse is a hinge: it forms the introduction to the second part of the song, the description of the conflict and the victory, in which Deborah throws herself into the great event she is about to commemorate. Keil adds a point of accent, that the imperative bears the tone on the last syllable the first two times, answering to the rapid summoning burst of the opening address.

Over the charge to Barak the two grammarians divide. Ellicott renders it lead in triumph thy long train of captives, comparing the phrase in the Revelation; Keil insists the words mean to lead away captives as the fruit of the victory, and not merely to lead in triumph. Clarke states it as a reversal — make those captives who have formerly captivated us. Henry takes it as a triumph in the Roman sense, and explains where the prisoners came from: though Sisera's army was cut off in the field and no quarter given, we may suppose that in the prosecution of the victory, when the war was carried into the enemy's country, many not found in arms were seized and made prisoners. These she would have led in chains after Barak when he made his public entry into his own city, to grace his triumph — not that it should be any pleasure to him to trample upon his fellow creatures, but that he must in this way give glory to God, and serve that great purpose of His government which is to look upon the proud and abase them.

Henry then turns to what the victory had made of the victors, and finds two improbabilities in it. The Israelites had become few and inconsiderable — many cut off by the enemy, many dead of grief, some having removed their families into foreign parts — and yet to that remnant God gave dominion over nobles, so that with one brave and generous effort they not only shook off the yoke from their own necks but got power over their oppressors. As long as any of God's Israel remain, and a remnant He will have in the worst of times, there is hope, be it ever so small a remnant; for God can make him that remains, though it should be but one single person, triumph over the most proud and potent. The second improbability is Deborah herself. She was of the weaker sex, the sex that from the fall had been sentenced to subjection, and yet the Lord who is himself higher than the highest authorised her to rule over the mighty men of Israel, who willingly submitted to her direction, and enabled her to triumph over the mighty men of Canaan, who fell before the army she commanded. So wonderfully did He advance the low estate of His handmaid; a despised stone is made head of the corner, and this is the Lord's doing, and marvellous in our eyes.
13:
Keil sees the brave men of the nation streaming down from the mountains to fight in the valley of Jezreel, though the nation did not rise as one man against its oppressors — only a remnant of the noble and brave, with whom Jehovah went into the battle. Ellicott names the absentees: a remnant only, because at least six tribes — Judah and Simeon, Dan and Asher, Reuben and Gad — held aloof; and he warns that the translation, reading and punctuation of the verse are all uncertain, so that Ewald's Then descended a remnant of the nobles of the people may be nearer, with Jehovah descended to me among the heroes for the second clause. Gill keeps the received rendering and reads a reversal of fortune — the people who had been under Jabin's yoke, many of whom very probably died there, the few that remained being now raised to a high estate; Clarke refers the remnant more narrowly to Barak.

On Ephraim's root in Amalek Ellicott sets aside the Septuagint and Vulgate rendering, that Ephraim uprooted them in Amalek, for the sense that out of Ephraim came down those whose root is in Amalek — the tribe having rooted itself in the country which had been the stronghold of the Amalekites. What follows he takes for a sudden change of person: after thee, O Ephraim, came down Benjamin, mingled with thy people, the forces of little Benjamin almost lost in the crowded ranks of its powerful neighbour; and the phrase after thee, Benjamin seems to have become a war-cry of the tribe. Clarke reads the passage backwards instead, taking Deborah to mean that out of Ephraim and Benjamin had come eminent warriors — Joshua of Ephraim, who routed the Amalekites soon after Israel left Egypt, and Ehud of Benjamin, who slew Eglon — while Machir produced warriors, and Zebulun statesmen and men of literature. He judges that Deborah speaks of past wars, not of anything done on this occasion, since no persons from Gilead were present in the war with Jabin. Gill reports the same division: Ephraim, where Deborah dwelt, was the root and source of the expedition and sent a detachment to prevent the Amalekites joining the Canaanites, though the Jewish commentators generally refer the words to a past action and understand by the root Joshua.

The pen of the writer Ellicott will not allow. The words are literally they who draw with the staff of the scribe; but the staff can hardly mean a pen, it is not easy to say what use a pen would be in the gathering of clans to battle, and we have not the faintest indication of any literary pre-eminence in Zebulun. There can be little doubt the sense is they who lead with the staff of the marshal, since the officer named musters, and therefore counts and enrols, the host, the staff being his rod of power and ensign of office, as the vine-staff was of the Roman centurions. Keil rejects the pointing that gives my princes in the next verse, since neither Deborah nor Barak was of Issachar and it is nowhere stated that the Issacharites gathered round her as their leader, and takes the phrase about the feet to mean incessantly impelled, an irresistible enthusiasm for the battle. Clarke would sooner drop the vowel points and render it with his footmen or infantry, as the Alexandrian Septuagint understood it and as Luther, he thinks, perfectly hit it. Of Reuben's divisions Ellicott observes that the word might mean families, as the Septuagint has it, or factions, as the Vulgate understood it, but almost certainly means streams, the allusion being to the Jabbok and its affluents; and he hears a contemptuous play of words between Reuben's magnanimous decisions and his evanescent projects — he debated and stayed at home on frivolous pretences, as Sparta did in the days of Marathon.
16:
Why Reuben stayed among the sheepfolds Gill explains by what the tribe owned. Reuben abounded with flocks and herds, and had chosen the country beyond Jordan as suitable for them; at this critical juncture they judged it their best policy to abide by them, lest, should Jabin prevail, he might be provoked to fall upon them and take them away — so that the bleatings of their flocks and the whistlings of the shepherds sounded louder in their ears than the groans of Israel under oppression or the sounding of the trumpet. Ellicott sharpens the picture by two corrections. The sheepfolds are literally hurdles, the dual form being due to some method of their construction, whence the Vulgate renders it between two boundaries; and what Reuben stayed to hear was not the bleating of flocks but the sound of shepherds' flutes, the pastoral pipings of Homer's shepherds delighting in syrinx-pipes — a contrast between those peaceful flutings and the battle-horns they ought to have heard. Reuben sent magnanimous debates and promises, he adds, which only ended in sloth and vacillation: they decided to go, and stayed at home.

The reproach of Dan is put as a sudden question, which Ellicott finds very picturesque, rejecting as untenable the other rendering that asks why Dan feared the ships of the enemy. The possession of Joppa, one of the few seaports of Palestine, naturally influenced the pursuits of the tribe, though whether they are reproached for absorption in commerce or for cowardice in taking refuge aboard is uncertain. He draws a chronological inference besides: if the Danite migration northward had by then occurred, it is almost impossible they should not have rendered some assistance to the northern revolt, and the fact that no allusion is made to it shows the extremely early date of the narrative. Clarke divides the blame by circumstance — the Gadites of Gilead could not well come at a short summons, but the words imply a criminal neglect in the Danites, who were intent on their traffic and trusted in their ships, while Asher, whose lot ran along the Mediterranean next to Zebulun and Naphtali, might easily have succoured them, pleading instead that his own posts were unguarded. On Asher's breaches Ellicott notes that the word is literally clefts, that the Chaldee curiously paraphrases it as the cities which the Gentiles destroyed, and that Le Clerc makes it his precipitous rocks, referring it to the Ladder of Tyre; the creeks of our margin is probably right.

Against all this Keil sets the two tribes that did come. Zebulun showed itself a people that despised its life even to death, sacrificing it for the deliverance of its fatherland, and Naphtali did the same in its mountain home; between them they raised the ten thousand fighting men who answered Barak's call and formed the kernel of the army. Clarke finds the Hebrew more emphatic than our word for it: they desolated their lives to death, being determined to conquer or die, and therefore plunged into the thickest of the battle — whereas jeoparded, he complains, is a silly French term, taken from the exclamation of a disappointed gamester, jeu perdu, the game is lost. Keil is troubled by a silence rather than a reproach, since Judah and Simeon are named neither among those who fought nor among those who stayed away; the only explanation he can find is that Barak never summoned them, either because they were too involved in conflict with the Philistines to help the northern tribes, or because of some inward disagreement between them and the rest. Of the enemy Ellicott notes only that they took not so much as a fragment of silver, though they had doubtless hoped, if not for much actual spoil, at least for ransom from the captives they expected to win, or for the gain of selling them into slavery.
20:
What fought from heaven they will not overstate. Keil says the words explain the earlier statement that the Lord discomfited Sisera, though not clearly enough to let us define the phenomenon by which God threw the enemy into confusion; in all probability it was a terrible storm, with thunder and hail, or the sudden bursting of a cloud, poetically described as though the stars of heaven had left their courses to fight for the Lord's kingdom upon earth. Ellicott makes the subject impersonal — the powers above — and holds the stars to be a general reference to the providential storms that secured the victory, warning that to take them for angels is a mistaken inference from Job; he finds a striking parallel in Claudian, where the sky serves as a soldier for the emperor and the winds come sworn together at the trumpet call. Clarke thinks a thunderstorm or inundation of the Kishon was attributed to the stars in poetic language, as an English poet made winds and waves conspire to aid old England against the Spanish armada.

Gill gathers the evidence. Many of the routed army, in their confusion, very probably tried to ford or swim it and were swept away and drowned, the waters swelling either in a miraculous manner, as Ben Gersom thinks, or through the large showers of rain that fell; and he cites Maundrell, who found the Kishon low and inconsiderable, but who, passing along the plain, discovered the track of many lesser torrents falling into it from the mountains, which must needs make it swell exceedingly upon sudden rains. Keil adds the direction of the rout: the battle being fought south of the brook and the smitten fleeing north, many met their death in waves then flowing over the banks; and he takes the brook's name to mean the stream of the olden world, flowing from time immemorial, rather than, as the Chaldee has it, the stream celebrated of old for the mighty acts performed there. Ellicott notes that from this slaughter, or that of the priests of Baal, the Kishon is now called the river of slaughter, and that it must always have played its part in the battles of the plain of Jezreel — as when the Turks drowned in its swollen waves in 1799.

The broken hoofs Clarke explains from the state of ancient horses: they were not shod then, nor are they to this day in several parts of the East; Sisera's, strongly urged on by those who drove them, had their hoofs broken by the roughness of the roads, so that they went lame and could not carry off their riders — marked here as one cause of the disaster. Ellicott prefers stampings to pransings, notes that the word is forcibly repeated by the figure called anadiplosis, and reports that crossing the Kishon after moderate rains he saw how easily a horse might be hopelessly disabled in the morass the river forms; the mighty ones he takes for the great lords in their iron chariots, goading their frightened steeds through the flood, with a scathing taunt in the phrase, their might being exhibited in valiantly running away. On the cursing of Meroz Gill holds that Deborah spoke under a spirit of prophecy, not from her own spirit in any revengeful way, and reports the guesses at what Meroz was — a star, Sisera's star; the name of a mighty man, as Jarchi has it; or, more likely, a town near the battlefield, which some identify with Merom. Ellicott judges its guilt worse than that of the tribes who held aloof, since it lay in the heart of the country and might at least have cut off the enemy's retreat: its crime was the refusal of military service, which the ancients regarded with special indignation, and he conjectures from the ban that it was destroyed like Succoth.
24:
Gill sets the blessing against the curse just pronounced: under the same influence Meroz is cursed and Jael blessed, the one for not helping Israel publicly, the other for doing it in private — and the blessing is pronounced either as a prayer that it might be so or as a prophecy that it should be, and indeed both. Keil marks how far outside Israel she stood, a woman of the Kenites, a tribe only allied with Israel; for her heroic deed she was to be blessed before women, the Hebrew meaning literally removed away from women, those in the tent being shepherdesses. Henry draws out what her choice cost her: she preferred peace with the God of Israel before peace with the king of Canaan, and though no native of Israel espoused their cause at the critical conjuncture, jeoparding her life as truly as if she had been in the high places of the field. From the closing phrase he takes a lesson for obscure service — those whose lot is cast in the tent, in a narrow sphere of activity, if they serve God there according to their capacity shall in no wise lose their reward, for Jael in the tent wins as rich a blessing as Barak in the field.

Whether the deed can be praised divides them sharply. Ellicott grants that Jael would be regarded as a patriotic heroine whose daring secured Israel the fruits of victory, but holds that the morals of that early age were not enlightened enough to understand that treachery and assassination are never justifiable, however good the end; and since serious moralists even in the nineteenth century have held up to admiration the murder of Marat by Charlotte Corday, and given her the title of the Angel of Assassination, we can hardly be surprised that Deborah should exult in Jael's heroism and her choice of the right side without any reprobation of the means. To compare this outburst of patriotic approval with the angel's salutation to the blessed Virgin, as some commentators do, seems to him a most dangerous way of handling the mere words of Scripture apart from their context. Clarke resolves the difficulty by narrowing the word: Jael shall be highly celebrated as a heroic woman, and the Israelitish women shall glory in her, but he does not take the words for the divine approbation, since to bless, in Hebrew and Greek alike, often signifies to praise, to speak well of, to celebrate, which is most probably its sense here.

The refreshment is described with care. Henry reads it as the kindness of a friend, which perhaps at the time she intended for nothing else, until God by an immediate impulse upon her mind directed her otherwise. Sisera asked only for fair water, but she, not merely to show her housewifery but to express respect, gave him milk and brought forth butter — which some take for milk with the butter taken out of it, and others for milk with the butter still in — and to set it off she brought it in a lordly dish, the finest she had, which confirmed his opinion of her friendship and made him sleep the faster and the more secure. Clarke observes that the Hebrew word signifies agitated, so buttermilk may be meant, which the Arabs make by agitating milk in a leathern bag and prize for its cooling quality; but he prefers cream, Sisera being not only thirsty but exhausted with fatigue. Deborah's point, he adds, is that Jael was more liberal than Sisera had asked: he requested water and she brought cream, not in an ordinary pitcher but in the most superb bowl she possessed. Keil calls the vessel a fine costly bowl such as they handed to noble guests, and Ellicott says plainly that it was all meant to lull his suspicions into a false security.
26:
How it was done Clarke reconstructs in two stages. Observing Sisera in a profound sleep, Jael took a workman's hammer, probably a joiner's mallet, and with one blow on the head deprived him of all sense; then she took a tent nail and drove it through his temples, pinning him to the earth — which she could not have done unless she had first stunned him. Gill fills in the details: it was her left hand that took the nail, as the Septuagint, Arabic and Vulgate all express it, and the nail was a pin of her own tent, that fastened it to the ground; and perhaps at her first approach Sisera rose up, but she had done the business so effectually at the first stroke that he dropped at once and laid his head down again. Keil describes the weapon as the hammer of the hard workers, a large heavy mallet, and observes that the words crowd together in the second half of the verse — to hammer, to smite in pieces, to dash in pieces, to pierce through — to depict the boldness of the deed.

Whether that crowding betrays something worse Ellicott takes up. The Hebrew, he says, is onomatopoetic, the sound echoing the sense and recalling the smashing blows of the hammer, and the repetition of these terrible alliterative verbs — hammered, shattered, battered, transfixed — with the signs that the prophetess revels in the description, have been ascribed to the delight of a satisfied thirst for revenge. That, he holds, is hardly a right view of her character. The feelings of modern times are far more refined than those of earlier ages, the value set on human life being immeasurably increased, whereas in ancient days no close moral analysis was applied to acts whose general tendency was approved as beneficial: Caesar was not inherently a cruel man, yet he records without a shudder the massacre of multitudes at Alesia, and suffered the brave Vercingetorix to be strangled in the Tullianum without a qualm of pity. Deborah, in the spirit of her day, regards the throes of Sisera's death with pitiless exultation only because she views the event in the single aspect of Israel's deliverance. Keil denies the charge outright: the heaping up of words is not the delight of a satisfied thirst for revenge, but simply brings out the thought that Sisera, for years the terror of Israel, was struck dead with a single blow. He also rejects the rendering that has Jael smite off his head, as does Clarke, who says the original does not warrant it — she smote his head, and transfixed him through the temples.

The falling Ellicott describes word by word, taking at her feet literally, as between her feet, as though the dauntless woman had stridden over him where he lay in the dead sleep of weariness; he bowed means that he suddenly curled his knees up in one contortion of agony, he fell that he rolled perhaps off the divan, he lay down that he was motionless after that one convulsive movement; and the last word is rather slaughtered, or murdered — with which one terrific word the scene ends, as with a blow. Then the scene changes with a bold poetic impetuosity, and Ellicott notes that Sisera's mother and her princesses watched for the host's return as the ladies of Aberdeen sat with their fans in their hands looking for the sails of Sir Patrick Spens; her cry is rather a wail, the Latin rendering an onomatopoeia like the Hebrew — the wail of impatience passing into anxiety. Gill will not have so much foreboding in it, and makes her watch not through fear of any ill but through impatience to see her son return in triumph, wreathed with laurels; Keil hears in her question a foreboding of the disastrous result of the war.
29:
The consolation offered by the attendant women is heard by all three as ironic. Ellicott gives the phrase literally as the wise of her princesses and finds unconcealed scorn in it, since the wisest proved the most mistaken, their wisdom being the seductive flattery of delusive hopes; the verb is singular, implying that one spoke after another, and the Vulgate renders it one of his wives, wiser than the rest. What follows he leaves undecided: it may mean that she repeats their answer to herself, accepting their flattering surmises, or on the contrary that she repeats her own words, entirely unconsoled — foreboding and inextinguishable hope being equally true to nature, according to the temperament of the Canaanite princess. Keil takes the second sense, that Sisera's mother would not be quieted by the words of her wise princesses but kept repeating the anxious question, and finds the irony obvious, since the reality put all their wise conjectures to shame. Gill is gentler with them: each in turn endeavoured to comfort her, and they seem to be her maids of honour, or ladies of her acquaintance come to share in the pleasing sight they expected.

What they imagine the delay to be Ellicott reads with a cold eye. A damsel or two is literally a maiden, two maidens, save that the word is strongly contemptuous, as though a captive Hebrew girl could only be described by a term of scorn; in these internecine wars the men were killed and the women reserved as slaves, and commentators quote Gibbon, who records that two or three Gothic female captives fell to the share of each of the soldiers of Claudius the Second. Nothing, he says, can exceed the power and skill with which in a few words the vanity, levity and arrogance of these wise princesses are set out, as they idly talk of colours and embroidery and, as it were, gloat over the description, while an unwomanly coarseness mingles with their womanly frivolity — only we must bear in mind that they too, like Deborah and Jael, though in an ignobler way, are the creatures of their age and circumstances.

The close comes abruptly, and Ellicott thinks the abruptness grand. The total frustration of the princesses' hopes is all the more forcibly implied by the scorn with which it is left unexpressed, and the single word so sums up the story in all its striking phases; that passionate exclamation accounts in part for the intensity of feeling which runs through the whole poem, by showing that Deborah regards the battle as part of one great religious crusade. He presses the comparison: when the warriors of the first crusade were riding deep in the blood of the murdered Saracens after the capture of Jerusalem, they were fully convinced that they were doing God service, and were so filled with religious emotion that at vesper-time they all fell upon their knees with streaming tears — the general dissemination of pity, even for our worst enemies, being a very modern feeling, and still far from universal. He adds that the closing words about the land's rest are no part of the song but conclude the whole story, and that this is the last we hear of any attempt by the Canaanites to reconquer what they had lost. Keil reads the same conclusion forward rather than back: the so refers to the whole song, meaning just in the same manner as Sisera and his warriors, and the rising of the sun in its strength is a striking image of the exaltation of Israel to a more and more glorious unfolding of its destiny, which Deborah anticipated as the result of this victory. Gill takes the last line as both a wish and a prediction — a prayer that God's enemies might so perish, and a prophecy that so they would.
